title: The First Morning
paragraphs: The first morning of middle school is strange. The building is bigger than my old school, and I do not know a single person in the corridor.
I find my classroom and choose a seat near the window. A girl sits down next to me and says, Hello, I am Lin Yue. What is your name?
That one question opens everything. We talk for twenty minutes about teachers we both know, and about a shop outside the school gate.
By the time the bell rings, I am not nervous any more. One question was enough. Her name is Lin Yue, and now I know three people in this room.

title: Ways to Say Hello
paragraphs: In English, hello is only the beginning. There are many ways to greet a person, and each one tells you something about the situation.
Hello and hi are neutral. You can use them with anyone. Hi is a little more casual, so students use it with friends and teachers who are relaxed.
Nice to meet you is used only the first time. The second time, you say nice to see you again. Mixing these two is a common mistake.
So a greeting is a small piece of social information. It says how close you are, what time it is, and whether this is the first meeting.

title: What I Say About Myself
paragraphs: When I introduce myself, I use four sentences. My name is Chen Hao. I am twelve years old. I am from Guangzhou. I like basketball.
My teacher says this is a good pattern because it is short and clear. But I notice that everybody gives the same four sentences.
The four sentences tell people who I am. The fifth sentence gives them something to ask about. That is the difference.
Now when I meet someone new, I still say the four sentences first. Then I wait. If they ask about the dog, we are going to be friends.

title: Names in English and Chinese
paragraphs: Chinese names put the family name first. English names put the given name first. This is the first thing to get right.
My name is Wang Mei. Wang is my family name and Mei is my given name. In English I write Mei Wang, and people call me Mei.
When you speak to a classmate, use the given name. Using the family name sounds distant, and using the full name sounds like a teacher calling the roll.
So a name carries two things at once: who you are, and how close the other person is allowed to be.

title: My Desk
paragraphs: My desk has three zones. The left side is for books, the right side is for the things I use every hour, and the middle is empty.
The middle being empty is the important part. If I put a pen there, I will lose it in two days. If the space is clear, I always know where to look.
The left side holds textbooks, standing up, with the spine facing out. I can find any book without lifting one.
This system takes ten minutes to set up and thirty seconds a day to keep. Before I had it, I spent five minutes every morning looking for my maths book.

title: Where Things Are
paragraphs: English uses three main words for position: in, on and under. They are small, but they carry most of the information.
In means inside something with a boundary. The pen is in the bag. The book is in the drawer. The cat is in the box.
There are two more you will need. Next to means beside, and between means in the middle of two things.
If you can use these five words, you can describe any classroom in the world. That is a lot of power for five short words.

title: The Lost Pencil Case
paragraphs: On Monday I lost my pencil case. I looked in my bag, on my desk and under my chair. It was not there.
I asked the boy behind me. He said he had not seen it. I asked the girl next to me. She said the same thing.
The strange part is this: nothing was missing. The pens, the ruler, the eraser were all inside. Only the position had changed.
I put a label on it that afternoon. A name does not stop you from losing a thing, but it does help the person who finds it.

title: What Is in My School Bag
paragraphs: My school bag weighs about four kilos. Last week I emptied it on the floor to see why.
There were six textbooks, two notebooks, a pencil case, a water bottle and a lunch box. That is the normal part.
I took out everything I had not used in two weeks. The bag went down to two and a half kilos.
A heavy bag is not always a sign of hard work. Sometimes it is just a sign that nobody has looked inside it for a month.
I emptied mine on the floor once. Half of it went into the bin, and I did not miss any of it.

title: A Place for Everything
paragraphs: Mum: Your room is a mess again. Where are your sports shoes?
Tom: Under the bed, I think. Or in the box by the door.
Mum: Which one? Go and look, please.
Tom: (after a minute) They are in the box. But only one of them.
Mum: Then find the other one before dinner. And Tom, put the books back on the shelf, not on the chair.
Tom: All right. Can I do it after dinner? Mum: No. A place for everything, and everything in its place.
Tom: And the shoes? Mum: In the box by the door, where they belong.
Tom: All right, all right. I am doing it now.

title: The Map at the Gate
paragraphs: There is a map of the school next to the main gate. Most students walk past it every day and never look at it.
The map shows four teaching buildings, a library, a dining hall, a playground and two gardens. The buildings are numbered, not named.
The map also shows the fire exits. In an emergency, that is the most important information on it.
On my first day, I stood in front of that map for five minutes. Now I could draw it from memory. That is what a school becomes after a few months.

title: Welcome to Our School
paragraphs: Last Friday some primary school students came to visit. I was one of the guides.

At the end they said thank you and went back to their school. I stood at the gate and remembered that I had asked the same questions a year ago.

title: Places in a School
paragraphs: Every school has the same basic places, and each one has a rule that students learn without being told.
The classroom is for lessons. You speak when the teacher invites you to. The library is for reading. You speak in a low voice, or not at all.
The office is for problems. You knock first, and you say what you need in one sentence.
The rule behind all these rules is the same: a place tells you how to behave. Learn the place, and you learn the manners.

title: The Garden Behind the Library
paragraphs: Behind the library there is a small garden that nobody uses. It has four benches, a lot of grass and one tree.
I found it in October, when I was looking for a place to read. It was quiet, and the tree made shade in the afternoon.
A teacher told us that the garden used to be a car park. Somebody planted the tree thirty years ago, and after that nobody wanted to cut it down.
I like that. A place changed because one person would not remove one tree.

title: First Day, Second Time
paragraphs: This year I helped with the first day of school. I stood at the gate with a sign and answered questions.
A boy came up and asked where Class Seven was. I told him, and then I saw his face. He was not listening. He was looking at the crowd.
He said thank you at the door and went in. I do not know if he remembered any of it.
But I remembered my own first day, and how one person walking with me made the building smaller.
So I walked over and said, I am new too. It was not true. It worked anyway.

title: The Friend I Did Not Choose
paragraphs: The teacher put me next to Zhou Yang in September. We did not choose each other. We were simply given the same desk.
For two weeks we said almost nothing. He drew cars in the corner of his notebook. I read. We shared a ruler when one of us forgot.
I still do not care about engines. But I liked how much he cared. That was the beginning.
Two years later he is the person I call first. We were not matched by interest. We were matched by a seating plan, and then by time.

title: What Makes a Friend
paragraphs: People say a friend is someone who helps you. That is true, but it is not complete. A stranger can help you too.
A friend is someone who knows what you are like when you are not being polite. That takes time, and it takes being seen in bad moments.
And a friend is someone who tells you the truth, but not all of it at once. Timing is part of honesty.
So friendship is not a feeling that arrives. It is a record of small things: shared desks, borrowed rulers, and days when nothing happened.

title: My Best Friend and I
paragraphs: My best friend and I are almost opposites. She talks to everyone. I talk to four people. She decides in a minute. I decide in a week.
This should be a problem, and sometimes it is. She makes plans I do not want. I say nothing, and then she is angry that I said nothing.
Our rule is simple: if one of us says I really do not want to, the other one stops asking. No explanation needed.
That rule took two years to build. It is worth more than the things we have in common.

title: A Letter to a New Classmate
paragraphs: Dear New Classmate,
Welcome to Class Three. I am the person who sits by the door, so you will probably meet me first. Here is what nobody tells you.
Mr Huang checks homework on Monday, so do it on Sunday night, not Monday morning. The PE teacher does not care about speed, only about trying.
You do not have to make friends in the first week. Most of us were alone in September. It sorts itself out by October.
If you get lost, ask anyone. Nobody here minds.
Yours, Chen Yu

title: Names and Nicknames
paragraphs: In my class, almost everybody has two names. The one on the register, and the one people actually use.
Nicknames come from three places. Some come from a physical habit: the boy who always taps his pen is called Drummer.
Some come from a mistake. My friend wrote his name wrong on a test in Grade Five, and the wrong version has followed him ever since.
A nickname is not always kind, but it is always a kind of attention. When a class stops making nicknames for you, that is when you should worry.

title: Four People and One Kitchen
paragraphs: There are four people in my family, and one kitchen. The kitchen is where everything happens.
My father cooks on weekdays because he gets home first. My mother cooks on Sunday because she says he uses too much oil.
I set the table. I have done it since I was seven, so I do it without thinking. Four bowls, four pairs of chopsticks, one small dish of chilli.
Nobody in my family talks about love. They cook, they set the table, they say eat more. That is the same sentence, said differently.

title: The Family Photo on the Wall
paragraphs: There is a photo on our wall of eleven people. I know nine of them. The other two died before I was born.
My grandmother can name everyone, and she can tell you the year and the reason for the photo. It was taken at my uncle's wedding.
I look at the photo sometimes when I am bored. Everybody is standing very straight, nobody is smiling, and everybody is wearing their best clothes.
It is strange to think that one day I will be the person explaining this photo to someone who was not born yet.

title: Words for Family
paragraphs: English family words are much less exact than Chinese ones. This causes real confusion for students.
In Chinese, your father's brother and your mother's brother have different names. In English, both are uncle.
If the detail matters, English adds words: my cousin on my mother's side, my older cousin. It takes longer, but it is clear.
This is a good example of a general rule: a language is exact where its speakers need to be exact, and vague everywhere else.

title: My Grandfather's Shop
paragraphs: My grandfather ran a small shop for thirty-eight years. It sold oil, salt, soap, batteries and newspapers.
He opened at six and closed at nine. He knew every family on the street, and he knew what they would buy before they asked.
He retired last year. The shop is a laundry now.
I asked him once if he was sad. He said, no. Thirty-eight years is a long time to stand in one place. Then he asked me about my exams.
I did not answer. I was thinking about thirty-eight years, and about the day he would lock the door for the last time.

title: The Library Rule
paragraphs: Our library has one rule that is not written anywhere: the third floor is for silence, the second floor is for group work.
Nobody told me this. I learned it in my first week, by sitting on the third floor with two friends and being looked at.
I have used that system ever since. When I need to think, I go up. When I need to talk, I go down.
Good buildings do this. They do not need signs for everything, because the people inside them agree on how to use the space.

title: A Day of Rooms
paragraphs: A school day is really a tour of rooms, and each room changes how you behave.
You start in the classroom, where you sit in the same seat and speak when called. Then you move to the lab, where you stand, touch things and follow safety rules.
In the afternoon you might go to the art room, where being wrong is allowed, or the music room, where being loud is required.
By four o'clock you have been six different people. This is one reason school is tiring: it is not one place, it is seven.

title: The New Building
paragraphs: Our school opened a new building in September. It has four floors, a lift and a roof garden.
At first everybody wanted to have a lesson there. After a month, nobody did, because the lift broke and the stairs are steep.
Only Class Eight is allowed up there, because their teacher is in charge of the plants. Everybody else complains about this.
I think the complaining is fair. But I also think a school should have one place that is not for everybody. It gives people something to work towards.

title: Directions Inside a Building

title: Six Twenty

title: Why Teenagers Sleep Late
paragraphs: Parents often say teenagers are lazy in the morning. Science says something different.
During the teenage years, the body clock shifts later by about two hours. The hormone that makes you sleepy is released later at night.
The problem is that school starts at the same time as before. The result is a permanent small sleep debt during the week.
This is why many doctors suggest later start times for secondary schools. It is not about comfort. It is about attention, mood and memory.

title: A Day in Two Countries

title: Why We Have Birthdays
paragraphs: A birthday marks a day that is not special in any natural way. The earth does not notice it.
Its meaning is entirely social. It says: we are glad you exist, and we are counting.
The counting is the interesting part. For a child, a birthday is a gain. For an older person, it can feel like a subtraction.
So the same date carries opposite meanings depending on where you are in life. This is why birthday wishes are careful.
In the end, a birthday is a yearly reminder that other people are keeping track of you. That is worth a cake.

title: Dates and Ordinal Numbers
paragraphs: Talking about birthdays requires two things that Chinese speakers often mix up: months and ordinal numbers.
There are twelve months. In English they are always written with a capital letter, and they are never numbered in speech.
The pattern for ordinals is regular except for the first three and the ones ending in them: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, then 4th to 20th all take th.
A common mistake is saying May one. It is understood, but it sounds like a page number, not a date.
So: on the fifth of May, or on May the fifth. Both are right. May five is not.

title: Why Some Animals Live in Groups
paragraphs: Many animals live in groups, and the reason is usually one of three: safety, food, or warmth.
Safety comes first. A single small animal is easy to catch. In a group, somebody is always watching while the others eat or sleep.
Warmth matters for animals in cold places. Penguins stand close together and take turns on the outside of the group.
So a group is not just company. It is a survival tool, and most animals that live alone have some other protection.

So the question is not whether zoos are good or bad. The question is what standard we accept.
My own view is simple. If the animal can be returned to the wild, the zoo is doing a job. If it can only live in the cage, we are keeping it for ourselves.

title: The Rule Nobody Likes

title: Why Rules Need Reasons
paragraphs: A rule without a reason lasts until the person in charge leaves the room.
If a teacher says, do not run in the corridor, students will run when the teacher is not there. If the teacher says, the floor is wet and people fall, the rule travels with them.
There is a second condition. The rule should apply to everyone, including the person who made it.
A rule that only binds the young is not a rule. It is a demand, and demands are obeyed only while somebody is watching.

title: Signs and What They Mean
paragraphs: Public signs are a short form of writing, and they work in a particular way.
Most signs use the imperative: Stop. No Entry. Keep Off the Grass. The verb comes first because the reader may be walking past.
Some signs give information rather than orders: Exit, Push, Emergency Phone. These are read in a hurry, so they are always short.
The test of a good sign is whether a stranger can understand it in one second. If it needs a second reading, it is badly made.

title: Traffic Rules in Two Cities
paragraphs: Traffic rules look the same everywhere, but the way people follow them is not.

There is also a design factor. A crossing with a countdown timer is followed better than one without, because people know how long they must wait.

title: How Much Exercise Is Enough
paragraphs: Doctors usually recommend one hour of activity a day for children and teenagers. That sounds like a lot.
But the hour does not have to be sport. Walking to school counts. Climbing stairs counts. PE lessons count.
What matters is the heart rate. Activity that makes you breathe faster for ten minutes or more is the kind that helps.
Strength matters too, but less for young people. Two sessions a week of climbing, carrying or jumping is enough.
So the target is not an hour of training. It is an hour of not sitting still, spread across the day.

title: Sleep Is Part of Training
paragraphs: Athletes train hard and sleep harder. Most of them sleep nine or ten hours, and they treat it as a session, not a rest.
The reason is that the body repairs itself during deep sleep. Muscle grows at night, not in the gym.
Students who train and sleep six hours are doing half the work. They also get injured more often.
The same is true for the brain. What you study in the evening is sorted and stored while you sleep.
So staying up to revise is a bad trade. You gain one hour and lose the process that makes the hour useful.

title: Breakfast
paragraphs: Breakfast is the meal students skip most often, and it is the one that matters most before a school day.
After eight hours without food, blood sugar is low. The brain runs on glucose, so attention and mood both drop.
Sweet drinks and cakes give a fast rise and a fast fall. Students who eat only that are hungry again by ten.
Ten minutes is enough time to eat properly. The problem is usually not time. It is that nobody got up ten minutes earlier. That small choice changes the morning.

title: Food Words in English
paragraphs: Talking about food in English needs three kinds of words, and students often learn only the first.
The first is the name of the food: rice, noodles, pork, cabbage. These are easy and there are many of them.
The second is the way it is cooked: fried, boiled, steamed, roasted, stir-fried. One food can have five names.
The third is the amount: a bowl of, a plate of, a slice of, a spoonful of. English counts food by container, not by piece.
This is why a bowl of rice sounds natural and a rice sounds wrong. The container is part of the word.

title: Why Diets Fail
paragraphs: Most diets fail, and the reason is not weak willpower. It is that a diet is a temporary rule applied to a permanent habit.
If you eat differently for six weeks and then stop, the old pattern comes back in a month. Nothing has actually changed.
The plans that work are boring. They change one thing: fewer sweet drinks, or a smaller bowl, or fruit instead of biscuits.
One change is easy to keep. Ten changes are a project, and projects end.
So the question is not what to give up. It is what you can still be doing in two years.

title: What Is Happening Now
paragraphs: English has a tense for things happening at this moment: the present continuous. It is built with be plus ing.
The form is simple, but the meaning needs care. It describes an action in progress, not a habit.
Some verbs rarely take this form. Know, want, like and believe describe states, not actions. Saying I am knowing is wrong.
There is one more use. It can describe a temporary situation: I am staying at my aunt's this week. Next week, I will be home.
So the tense is not only about now. It is about anything that is still open.

title: Why It Rains
paragraphs: Rain begins with evaporation. The sun heats water in the sea, the rivers and the soil, and some of it turns into vapour.
Warm air rises, carrying the vapour with it. As it rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much water.
Inside the cloud the droplets bump into each other and join. When one is heavy enough, it falls.
If the air below is very cold, it falls as snow. If it passes through a warm layer and then a cold one, it falls as hail.
So rain is not water falling from nowhere. It is water going up, and then coming back down.

title: Four Seasons in One City
paragraphs: Guangzhou has four seasons on paper, but the paper is optimistic.
Spring is warm and wet. The walls sweat, clothes do not dry, and everything smells of damp for about six weeks.
Winter is mild and grey. It rarely goes below ten degrees, but there is no heating indoors, so it feels colder than the number says.
So the year is really two seasons and two short transitions. The calendar says four because calendars are made for the whole country. Here, the weather has its own schedule.

title: What to Wear
paragraphs: Amy: What is the weather like in Beijing in October?
Ben: Cold in the morning, warm at noon. About eight degrees at seven, and twenty at two.
Amy: So what do I wear? Ben: A T-shirt and a jacket. You will take the jacket off by eleven.
Amy: And at night? Ben: Colder than you expect. Bring something warmer than you think you need.
Amy: Should I bring an umbrella? Ben: Yes. It does not rain often, but when it does it is cold rain.
Amy: And a hat. Ben: Now you sound like my mother.

title: The Weather and My Mood
paragraphs: People say rain makes them sad. I think it is more exact than that: rain makes people stay in, and staying in makes some people sad.
The weather itself does very little. What changes is what we do. A rainy day cancels a football match and leaves an afternoon empty.
This matters because it gives us a choice. If the problem is the empty afternoon, the answer is a plan, not sunshine.
I keep a list of things to do on rainy days. It is a short list, and it has never failed.

title: Before the Storm
paragraphs: There is a moment before a summer storm when everything goes still. The wind stops, the birds stop, and the air feels heavy.
Then the temperature drops. You can feel it on your arms before you see anything.
The first drops are large and separate. They hit the dust and make small dark circles.
Then the whole sky arrives at once. The rain is not falling in drops any more; it is falling in sheets.
Ten minutes later it is over. Steam comes off the road. Somebody opens a window, and the whole street smells of wet cement.

title: The Umbrella
paragraphs: I bought an umbrella in June and lost it in July. This happens to me twice a year.
The strange thing is that I never lose anything else. Not my keys, not my wallet. Only umbrellas.
A friend explained it. An umbrella is the only object you carry only when you do not need it visible. It hangs, it gets put down, it stays.
So I bought a very ugly one, bright orange, with a broken handle. I could not leave it anywhere without noticing.
I have had it for fourteen months. It is the longest relationship I have had with an umbrella.

title: The Day I Got Lost
paragraphs: I got lost in Hong Kong when I was nine. It lasted about forty minutes, and it felt like a week.
I was following my father through a market. I stopped to look at a stall selling toys, and when I turned round, he was gone.
After a while a woman in a shop asked if I was alone. She let me sit on a stool inside and gave me water.
My father came back eleven minutes later. He had run three streets. He did not shout at me. He just said, good, you stayed.

title: Why We Remember Some Days
paragraphs: Most days disappear. A few stay for decades. The difference is not how good or bad the day was.
The first factor is novelty. A new route, a new food, a first time doing anything makes the brain record more detail.
The third is story. If a day has a shape, with a beginning and an end, it is easier to keep. That is why we remember the day we got lost but not the day we did homework.
So a memorable day is not necessarily a happy one. It is one that was different, felt strongly, and can be told.

title: The Last Day of Primary School
paragraphs: On the last day of primary school, we were told to clean the classroom. Nobody wanted to, and everybody did it anyway.
We took down the posters and found six years of marks on the wall. Somebody's name was written behind a map in Grade Three.
Mine said: you talk too much in class, and the room is quieter when you are absent. I have thought about that sentence for years.
We left at noon. The gate was the same as always. I remember being surprised that it looked exactly the same.

title: A Trip I Would Do Again
paragraphs: In the summer of Grade Six, my family went to a small town in the north. There was nothing to see there. That was the point.
We stayed four days. We walked the same two streets every morning, ate at the same noodle shop, and sat by the river in the evening.
I have been to bigger places since. I remember very little of them, because we were always moving.
This is what I learned from that trip: four days in one place beats one day in four places. The town was boring, and that is why I remember it.

title: Telling a Story About a Day
paragraphs: Telling a story about a day needs three things: a time order, a turning point and a detail.
Time order is easy. Use first, then, after that, and finally. But do not use all of them; two or three are enough.
The detail is what makes it believable. Not the whole scene, one thing: the colour of a door, the sound of a bell, the price of a ticket.
A story with all three is short and clear. A story with only time order is a list, and nobody remembers a list.

title: The Sports Day

title: The Woodcutter and the Axe

title: Why Fairy Tales Begin with Once
paragraphs: Almost every fairy tale begins with once upon a time. The phrase does two jobs at the same moment.
First, it removes the story from the calendar. There is no year, so nobody can check whether it happened.
The ending has its own phrase: and they lived happily ever after. Both phrases are promises about the shape of the story.
This is why a fairy tale does not need a realistic setting. The opening has already told you what kind of world you are in.

title: The Three Wishes
paragraphs: A poor man was given three wishes. He went home and told his wife, and they argued about how to use them.
While they argued, he was hungry. He said, without thinking, I wish I had a sausage. A sausage appeared on the plate.
His wife was furious. She said, you wasted a wish on a sausage! I wish the sausage was on your nose!
The sausage jumped onto his nose, and stuck there.
So they used the third wish to get it off. That evening they had nothing but a sausage, and they were laughing too hard to eat it.

title: The Fox and the Crow
paragraphs: A crow found a piece of cheese and sat in a tree to eat it. A fox came and stood under the tree.
The fox said, good morning, beautiful bird. Your feathers are the finest I have seen. Surely your voice must be as fine.
The crow was pleased. She opened her beak to sing, and the cheese fell.
The fox caught it and said, that was all I wanted. Thank you for the lesson: never trust a person who praises you for no reason.
The crow learned something too. She never sang in a tree with food in her mouth again.

title: What Fairy Tales Teach
paragraphs: People say fairy tales are for children. The stories are simple, the good are rewarded, and the wicked are punished.
But the simple shape is doing a serious job. A child meets dishonesty, greed and jealousy for the first time in a story, not in life.
The danger is when the shape becomes a promise: be good and you will be rich. Real life does not work like that, and children discover it soon enough.
So the stories are not instructions. They are rehearsals. We practise judging people in a world where we cannot be harmed.

title: Reading to My Cousin
paragraphs: My cousin is five. She asks me to read the same book every night, and it is a very bad book.
The pictures are ugly and the story makes no sense. A bear steals a bicycle and rides it to the sea. That is the whole plot.
So I read it again, and I started changing things. The bear now has a name, a family and a reason for wanting a bicycle.
She has not noticed. She still thinks it is the same book. I have told the story eleven times and the bear has had four different jobs.

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
paragraphs: A shepherd boy was bored, so he ran to the village shouting that a wolf had come. The villagers ran up the hill with sticks. There was no wolf.
He did it again the next week. Again they came, and again there was nothing.
The third week a wolf really did come. The boy shouted, and nobody moved.
The villagers heard him. They had heard him before.
The story ends with the sheep, not the boy. This is the part people forget. The cost of a lie is not paid by the liar alone.
